D:\\wt\\lcfpoor\\vlog\\lcfpoor\\voz\\b00.text: This dented enamel pot is coming up off the stove, honey, lid and all. Cold nights are here, and a lot of us are eating supper alone. My mother fed seven of us out of this pot in 1938. Tonight it feeds one for about 40 cents. So what goes in it tonight? I'll tell you near the end, and you'll know it when you hear it. Stay with me, honey. Look in your cupboard, honey, behind the cereal. I'm Loretta, 81, cooking for one in Story County, Iowa. My mother's kitchen wasted nothing. Not a bone, not a can, not a potato. The same thinking feeds one of us tonight for pennies a plate. 25 suppers are coming. Stay for number 13, the spaghetti trick, and number 25, the payoff pot. Let's start with number one, and it starts with one can of tomatoes. number one, and I'll turn your thinking around. You figure a can means the lazy supper.

I wrote it plain on page 75. One can of tomatoes, half an onion, a tablespoon of butter, and a cup of broth. Soften the onion and the butter in one small pot. Add the rest and simmer. Mash it smooth with a potato masher. My trick is a pinch of sugar, which takes the sour edge off canned tomatoes. It is cheap honey and it makes two bowls. Stir in the milk off the heat so it never curdles. Then pour one bowl at a table set for one in the dented pot from the start. That's the pot I kept for suppers like this. My mother's pot sits on my back burner, honey. It's dented and it's the pot my mother fed seven of us out of. I still have it and I still cook in it. Nothing went to waste in that pot, then or now. Number two is one chicken thigh stretched into soup the way that pot always stretch things. Number two is one chicken thigh, honey. Most homes boil a whole bird for hours.

Here it's one thigh, three cups of water, and one small pot. Simmer it 25 minutes, then pull the meat off and toss the skin and bone. I wrote it plain on page 76. Cook the rice in the soup only if you'll eat it in two days. For the freezer, cook the rice apart and add it when you heat it. Chicken is done at 165 degrees. Two bowls that taste like sundae, honey. Got a saucepan sitting on your stove? Good, that's the one we want. Every one of these is one page of my little book, Supper for One, and the link is below in the description. If you missed my earlier one-pot video on this channel, it's waiting for you there. Missed my earlier video? Find 10 cheap one-pot suppers for seniors living alone the church lady way on this channel. Back to that 40 cent pot. Number three is a ham bone and a bag of split peas.

This is the cheapest bowl yet, honey, and it's pure hard-year sinking. Page 77. That bone simmers right along with the peas an hour and a half until they fall apart. Taste before you salt it. The ham is salty. It sets like cement in the fridge, so add a splash of water when you reheat it. Eat one bowl and freeze the rest in one-bowl bags. Eight bowls, about 35 cents a bowl. Number four is the fastest soup on this list, done in five minutes. Number four is for the night you can't face a stove. Broth, an egg, and that supper, page 78. Bring the broth to a boil and stir in the cornstarch water. Turn off the heat, then pour the beaten egg in a thin stream. Stir in one direction, honey, and the egg makes long ribbons instead of little crumbs. Look at the ribbons in the bowl. another no chopping night a bag from the freezer and a box of broth

Number five is for nights you don't want to chop. Mine is frozen mixed vegetables and a box of broth. Page 79. Bring the broth and tomatoes to a boil. Snap the spaghetti from the bottom of the box into the pot and cook six minutes. Those broken ends are the hard year's habit. Nothing wasted. Then the vegetables go in for four more. From the frozen vegetable bag to a bag of frozen broccoli and a little cheese. Number six is cheesy broccoli soup, page 80. Most homes dump in handfuls of mild cheese. My mother bought one block of sharp cheddar and grated it fine, honey. Sharp cheddar gives more taste with less cheese. Mild cheddar just makes it gluey. Simmer the broccoli eight minutes in the thickened broth and milk and it makes two bowls. From a bag of broccoli to a quarter pound of hamburger and a neighbor's winter soup.

Number seven is hamburger soup. Page 81, my neighbor Arlene's winter soup. Most folks stir the beef till it's gray. Don't do that, honey. Brown it hard until it's crusty. That brown is where the taste comes from. Add a potato, a carrot, a can of tomatoes, and two cups of broth. Ground beef must reach 160 degrees. Eat a bowl. Freeze two. From meat to no meat, a cup of pantry lentils that needs no soaking. Number eight is lentil soup for the pantry, page 82. Lentils need no soaking, honey, so decide at four and eat at five. Soften an onion, a carrot, and a celery rib in oil. Add the lentils, broth, half a can of tomatoes and cumin, and simmer 30 minutes. It makes four bowls for pennies a bowl, but it isn't the pot from the start. Tonight, reach for a potato, a can of corn, and a little bacon for a cold night.

Number nine is potato and corn chowder, page 83. Fry two slices of bacon in a small pot and lift half out for the top. Cook the onion in that fat, then add one diced potato and a cup of broth. Simmer until soft, then mash a few pieces against the pot. Mashing a few pieces of potato thickens chowder better than any flour. Stir in the corn and milk, the last soup, a can of white beans, and a little green chili. Number 10 is white chicken chili, page 84. Most folks reach for beef in October. Mine is a can of white beans, leftover chicken, and a small can of green chilies. Cook the onion, then simmer it all 15 minutes with the cumin. Pick the mild green chilies, honey. The jalapenos beside them are not mild. it makes three cheap bowls. Soups are done. Hand to the noodles and rice group, starting with the Iowa School Lunch Goulash.

Number 11, Iowa goulash, page 110. Most folks boil macaroni in a second pan. Mine cooks right in the sauce. Ground beef, tomatoes, a cup of water or broth, and dry elbow macaroni all go in together. Simmer it covered 12 minutes until the macaroni is soft. One pot to wash. It makes three plates. Eat one and freeze two. It's the school lunch everybody loved. From one pot of macaroni to one pot with three dumplings steaming under the lid. Number 12. Chicken and dumplings for one. Page 117. Most folks cook a crowd's pot. Mine starts with a cup and a half of broth and half a cup of leftover chicken. Stir a third cup of biscuit mix with two tablespoons of milk. Drop three spoonfuls on top and cover. Ten minutes, honey. Don't peak. The steam is what makes them light. Number 13 next, the spaghetti trick, where a little sauce covers a whole plate.

Number 13, Spaghetti for One, page 108. Here's the trick I promised. Not sauce on top, honey. Brown a quarter pound of beef, onion, and garlic in a small pot. Pour off the fat. Add a can of crushed tomatoes, a pinch of sugar, and the Italian seasoning. Simmer 15 minutes. Cook half the spaghetti, then toss it in the sauce with a splash of the pasta water. It clings, so you need less. Now hold up a bundle of dry spaghetti as thick as a quarter. That is one plate, honey. The page tells you the pot makes two plates, so freeze the other half in a bag. The 40-cent pot is still waiting, and so are the tired night noodles. Number 14, page 109, is for a tired night. Most homes cook the peas in a second pot. Here they ride in with the noodles for the last two minutes, one pot doing both. Use a cup and a half of dry noodles.

Drain, then toss with a tablespoon of butter, two of grated parmesan and pepper until it shines. Chop a little ham in, and it's a farm supper. Sit a minute, honey. Find last week's grocery bill, honey. Seven suppers from my book cost a good deal less than a week of frozen dinners, and that money stays in your purse. Point your phone at the little square on the screen for my book. The 40-cent pot and the end-of-the-month eggs are still ahead. Next, real macaroni on the stovetop. Number 15, Stovetop Macaroni and Cheese. Most homes melt the cheese in a second pan. My mother kept it all in one pot, on low. Three-quarters cup dry elbow macaroni, drained. Back in with butter, a third cup of milk, and three-quarters cup of cheddar. A pinch of mustard powder makes the cheese taste cheesier. You won't taste mustard. Eat it right away. It thickens as it sits.

D:\\wt\\lcfpoor\\vlog\\lcfpoor\\voz\\b01.text: Next, a quarter head of cabbage and a few inches of sausage. Number 16, kielbasa, cabbage and potatoes, page 90. Most homes let the rest slide to the back of the crisper. Here it's a quarter head and a few inches of sausage, browned first. Cook the potato and onion eight minutes, then the cabbage and a spoon of water, eight more. Sausage goes back in with a splash of vinegar. The rest keeps two weeks wrapped tight, the longest-keeping vegetable you can buy. Those leftover potatoes? Mama never let one go to waste. Number 17, page 89. My mother fried up every leftover potato in the house. Most homes let cold potatoes go soft in the bin. Cold-cooked potatoes fry better than fresh ones, so boil two extra every time. slice them into a hot skillet with a spoon of bacon grease, lay them flat and leave them alone five minutes then turn them with onion for eight more

Penny's a plate, honey. From the potato skillet to a quarter pound of hamburger made into a steak under onion gravy. Number 18, hamburger steak with onion gravy, page 87. Most homes roll the beef into a ball and it puffs up. Shape a quarter pound into an oval and press a thumb dent in the middle. It stays flat instead of puffing up, honey. Brown it four minutes a side. Soften half an onion in that pan, add flour, broth, and Worcestershire, and simmer the patty back in three minutes. Beef to 160 degrees. Last stop, eggs and beans for the end of the month. Number 19 is the supper for the end of the month. A cup of tomato sauce and two eggs poached right in it. Most homes at that point reach for the phone and call for takeout. Make two hollows with a spoon, crack an egg into each and cover the pan on low six to eight minutes until the whites are set.

In an Ohio winter, the windows are shut tight, the ceiling is cold because the attic above it is cold, and every shower turns into water on that ceiling. So a bathroom that was fine all summer gets spots by February. That's also why the spots are always in the same place. Right over the shower and in the corner by the outside wall where the ceiling is coldest.

Number 21, baked beans on toast, page 137. Most of us let the rest go cold in the can. Folks laughed at this one for years, and so did I. Then I tried it, warmed the beans with a spoon of mustard, and they taste homemade. Spoon them over buttered toast and top with cheese or a fried egg. 80 cents a plate. From half a can to yesterday's pot roast, chopped and fried crisp. Number 22, Pot Roast Hash, page 153. Most homes let Sunday's roast go dry in the fridge. Nothing from Sunday goes to waste. Crisp a quarter onion, add one cup of chopped roast and potatoes, and press it flat. Turn it in pieces, fry an egg on top, and spoon in that leftover gravy, honey. It's better than the first night. That dented pot from the start? Tonight it gets its supper for pennies. Number 23 pays off that dented pot.

Ham and bean soup from The Ham, page 155. The holidays are coming, and most of us toss the bone. I wrote it plain in my book. The bone and bits make two quarts. Simmer soaked navy beans with the bone, an onion and two carrots in eight cups of water until soft. Pull the meat off, put it back, and mash some beans against the pot. Six bowls, honey, for pennies a bowl. Let me tell you where a ham bone used to go. Nobody let a ham bone go to waste in my day, honey. After a holiday dinner, the bone went home with me in a paper sack, and that bone was a week of lunches. I carried that sack out to the car like a pie, from the church supper bone to a can of salmon and the Friday supper every grandmother made. Number 24. Salmon Patties A can of salmon makes four patties the way every grandmother made them on Friday.

Mix in an egg, a third cup of crushed crackers, and chopped onion. Those crackers stretch one can into four. Fry two in oil, four minutes a side, and sit down to one plate. The other two go in the freezer raw, between paper. Fry them from frozen, six minutes a side. Hand to the last one, three potatoes and a little bacon. Number 25, page 38. fry two slices of chopped bacon in the dented pot lift them out and leave the fat that fat carries the whole soup soften a quarter of an onion in it add three cubed potatoes and two cups of broth and simmer it mash about half the potatoes right in the pot stir in a cup of milk and heat it don't boil top your bowl with the bacon cheddar and green onions snipped off the windowsill the The whole pot makes three bowls and it freezes fine if you freeze it before the milk goes in.

Tonight that pot makes one bowl, and you eat it at a table set for one on a cold October night. Tonight, honey, one potato and one slice of bacon is all it takes. Tonight, open your cupboard and look for a box of broth and a can of tomatoes. Page 74 says always keep both on hand. Then set one place at your table with a napkin and a spoon. Then tell me about your own mother's pot down in the comments. Tell me what your mother put in her one pot when money was thin and do you still have that pot? Then go see my other channel where farm families never throw a thing away. If you have a minute go see 10 things Iowa farm families never throw away. Most Americans toss them every week. That one is on my other channel all about farm kitchens. Farm folks have kept that habit for a long, long time. Now, back to my little book. A cookbook for one doesn't have to be sad.

Supper for One has 140 small suppers, one page each, with the cost on every page. Set the table, use the good plate, and turn to any page. The link is in the description below. Next week, more small supper for you. Next week I've got more small suppers for one. So bring the good plate and pull up a chair, friend, and I'll see you soon. Light a candle tonight and use the good plate. call somebody while you eat honey bless you friend for setting a place for yourself at the table then set the lid back on the dented pot
